opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a great question, because AI wasn't an afterthought for us; it was there from the very beginning.

If you go back to the origins of Spark at Berkeley, in the AMPLab, one of the first motivating workloads was machine learning. Matei was working on it partly because people around us, including folks working on the Netflix Prize, wanted to run iterative algorithms over large datasets, and Hadoop MapReduce was terrible at that. Every iteration meant going back to disk. So Spark's in-memory design was really built with ML in mind. MLlib came very early.

When we started Databricks, the vision was to make big data simple, and the reason you want big data in the first place is to extract value from it. Ultimately that means analytics and machine learning, or what we'd now call AI. Data and AI were always two sides of the same coin for us. You can't do good AI without good data, and much of the value of data comes from the AI you build on top of it.

What has changed is the scale and the shape of the opportunity. Ten years ago, "AI" in the enterprise mostly meant classical ML: fraud detection, recommendations, forecasting. Most companies were still struggling to get their data in order, so a lot of our early work, like Delta Lake and the lakehouse architecture, was about building a solid data foundation. In hindsight, that foundation is exactly what you need now. With large language models and generative AI, the bottleneck for enterprises isn't really the model, since many good models are available. It's connecting those models to the company's own data in a way that's governed, secure, and high quality. That's precisely where Databricks sits.

So I'd say the current focus on AI isn't a pivot. It's more like the world catching up to where we always thought it would go. The difference is that the pace is much faster than anyone expected, and the applications, such as agents and natural-language interfaces to data, are richer than we imagined back then. But the core thesis, that data and AI belong on one platform, is the same one we started with.

r001.rationale: It says Databricks was founded to make big data simple so customers could extract value through analytics and machine learning, and calls the current AI focus a continuation of that thesis.

r002.rationale: It identifies machine learning as an early Spark workload and says Spark was designed for iterative algorithms over large datasets because Hadoop MapReduce handled those poorly.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's interesting, because when we started Databricks in 2013, the thesis was actually pretty simple. We believed that data and the computation on top of data were going to converge, and that the people who had the data would be the ones who could do the most interesting things with it. Spark came out of the AMPLab at Berkeley, and the "A" in AMP stood for algorithms, the "M" for machines, the "P" for people. So machine learning was there from the beginning. It wasn't an afterthought. MLlib was one of the first libraries we built on top of Spark.

What has changed is the scale and the kind of models. Back then, machine learning meant logistic regression, random forests, maybe some collaborative filtering for recommendations. Nobody was talking about models with hundreds of billions of parameters. But the fundamental insight was the same: the value is in the data, and the hard part is getting from raw data to something useful. That's still true. If anything, it's more true now, because these large models are only as good as what you feed them, and the differentiated data lives inside companies, not on the public internet.

So when I look at the current focus on AI, I see it as the natural continuation of what we set out to do. The lakehouse was about unifying data warehousing and data science so you didn't have to copy data between systems. Now the question is how you bring generative AI to that same data, in a way that's governed, that respects access controls, that an enterprise can actually trust. That's a data problem as much as it's a model problem. And honestly, that's where I think we have an advantage, because we never saw ourselves as a model company or a data company. We saw it as one thing.

The part that even I didn't fully anticipate was how fast the models themselves would become commoditized, and how much the differentiation would move back toward the data and the systems around it. But in a sense, that's the original bet paying off.

r001.rationale: It calls the current AI focus a “natural continuation” of the original vision and ties both to helping turn company data into useful outcomes.

r002.rationale: It says machine learning was present from the beginning and mentions MLlib and classical methods, but does not identify accelerating classical machine learning algorithms as a motivation for creating Spark.

astra-6.text:
I see it as a natural continuation of the original vision. The idea was to help organizations get value from their data. AI is one of the most powerful ways to do that, but it depends on having the right data and being able to work with it effectively.

So, from that perspective, the focus on AI doesn’t change the fundamental goal. It expands what you can do. You want to make it easier to go from data to something useful—whether that’s an insight, a prediction, or an application—and reduce the complexity along the way.

r001.rationale: The response calls Databricks’ AI focus a natural continuation of its original vision to help organizations get value from their data.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Spark or accelerating classical machine learning algorithms as an original motivation.

sol-6.1.text:
I see it as a natural evolution of the original vision. We wanted to make it easier for organizations to get value from their data. Initially, a lot of that meant processing large datasets and making analytics and machine learning more accessible. With AI, the goal is still the same, but the possibilities are much broader.

The connection is data. If you want to build AI that is useful for your business, it needs to work with your data, and you need to manage that data reliably and securely. So bringing data and AI together is very consistent with why we started the company.

r001.rationale: It says the original goal was helping organizations get value from their data and describes AI as a broader continuation of that goal.

r002.rationale: It mentions making machine learning more accessible, but does not identify accelerating classical machine learning algorithms as a motivation for creating Spark.
